Text: The endocrine glands that regulate sexual function, characteristics, and reproduction are the {{c1::ovaries}}, in the {{c2::female pelvis}}, producing {{c3::estrogen}}, and the {{c1::testes}}, in the {{c2::male scrotum}}, producing {{c3::testosterone}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: ovaries and testes are the paired sex glands — the same endocrine job, mirrored across the sexes.

Distinguish: the ovaries sit within the pelvis, while the testes hang outside the pelvic cavity in the scrotum.

Text: The kidneys lie on the {{c1::posterior::anterior or posterior}} muscular wall of the abdomen, in the {{c2::retroperitoneal space::body region}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: retroperitoneal means behind the peritoneum, so the whole urinary system sits behind the organs of the digestive system.

Distinguish: the pancreas occupies that same space, which is why it is fixed deep in the abdomen and not easily damaged.

Text: Blood flow through the kidneys is high — nearly {{c1::20%}} of the blood pumped out by the heart passes through the kidneys each minute.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the liver takes an even larger share of the cardiac output each minute.

Why: the kidneys filter continuously to clear toxic waste and hold the balance of water and salts, so they need an outsized share of the circulation.

Text: The {{c1::renal pelvis::kidney structure}} is the {{c2::cone-shaped collecting area inside the kidney}}, where the urine-carrying tubes unite before funneling urine through the {{c3::ureter}} into the bladder.
Back Extra:
Pathway: kidney tubules → renal pelvis → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra → outside the body.

Cue: each kidney normally drains into just one ureter, and the two ureters enter the bladder posteriorly at its base.

Text: {{c1::Peristalsis}} is the {{c2::wavelike contraction of smooth muscle}} that moves urine through the ureters into the bladder.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: peristalsis also drives the digestive tract, where the same wave moves food along; in the urinary system the squeezing is done by the ureters.

Why: the ureters are narrow, hollow, muscular tubes — the muscle in their walls is what actively drives urine toward the bladder.

Text:
The male reproductive system consists of six organs:
{{c1::testicles}}
{{c1::epididymis}}
{{c1::vasa deferentia}}
{{c1::prostate gland}}
{{c1::seminal vesicles}}
{{c1::penis}}
Back Extra:
Cue: only the prostate gland and the seminal vesicles lie inside the pelvic cavity — the rest of the male genitalia lie outside it.

Pathway: immature sperm leave the testicles → epididymis to develop → vasa deferentia → seminal vesicles for storage → urethra at ejaculation.

Text:
The female reproductive system consists of five organs:
{{c1::ovaries}}
{{c1::fallopian tubes}}
{{c1::uterus}}
{{c1::cervix}}
{{c1::vagina}}
Back Extra:
Pathway: a mature egg leaves an ovary → fallopian tube, where fertilization normally occurs → uterus; the cervix is the narrow opening from the uterus into the vagina.

Cue: apart from the clitoris and labia, the female genitalia sit entirely within the pelvis.

Text: {{c1::Aerobic metabolism::process}} is {{c2::energy production that uses oxygen::meaning}}, and its waste products are {{c3::carbon dioxide and water}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: anaerobic metabolism, literally without air, runs with no oxygen, yields far less energy, and leaves lactic acid, the burn felt in muscles during heavy lifting.

Cue: aerobic literally means with air, so the oxygen requirement is built into the name.

Text: Aerobic metabolism supplies a cell with about {{c1::15 times::multiple}} more ATP than the same cell can make without oxygen.
Back Extra:
Why: with oxygen the cell can run nutrients all the way down to carbon dioxide and water, while without oxygen it stops at lactic acid and captures only a fraction of the energy.

Meaning: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the molecule cells use to store and spend energy.

Text: Most cells can run on anaerobic metabolism, which makes energy without oxygen, for only about {{c1::1 to 3 minutes::duration}}, while {{c2::heart and brain::2 organs}} cells cannot survive without a constant supply of oxygen.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: brain cells are the strictest of all, beginning to die after only 4 to 6 minutes without oxygen.

Why: as lactic acid and other wastes pile up around the cells the area turns toxic, cells die, whole organs fail, and the patient can go into cardiac arrest.

Text: Deprived of oxygen, brain cells begin to die after only {{c1::4 to 6 minutes::duration}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: ordinary cells can hold out on anaerobic metabolism for about 1 to 3 minutes, while heart and brain cells cannot survive any interruption in oxygen supply.

Cue: 4 to 6 minutes is the number behind every airway-and-breathing-first habit in EMS.

Text: Blood carries carbon dioxide by combining it with water into {{c1::carbonic acid::compound}}, and plasma neutralizes that acid with alkaline {{c2::sodium bicarbonate::compound}}.
Back Extra:
Why: carbonic acid dissolves in plasma far more readily than carbon dioxide gas does, so the conversion is what lets blood carry the waste at all.

Mechanism: the lungs then set blood pH by how much carbon dioxide they blow off, since less carbon dioxide leaves less carbonic acid behind.

Text: {{c1::Respiratory compromise::condition}} is {{c2::the inability to move gas effectively::meaning}}, leaving the patient hypoxic, hypercapnic, or both.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: breathing has two halves, ventilation (moving air between the lungs and the environment) and respiration (gas exchange at the membrane), and working out which half failed is what points to the cause.

Distinguish: hypoxic means the oxygen level has fallen, hypercapnic means the carbon dioxide level has risen, and either one alone is enough to call it compromise.

Text: Respiratory compromise produces {{c1::hypoxia::condition}}, which is {{c2::a decreased oxygen level in the body::meaning}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: hypercapnia is the opposite pole of the same problem, an elevated carbon dioxide level, and a compromised patient can have one, the other, or both.

Mechanism: starved of oxygen, cells drop from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism and start pouring out lactic acid.

Text: Respiratory compromise produces {{c1::hypercapnia::condition}}, which is {{c2::an elevated carbon dioxide level in the body::meaning}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: hypoxia is the opposite pole of the same problem, a decreased oxygen level, and a compromised patient can have one, the other, or both.

Mechanism: rising carbon dioxide means more carbonic acid in the blood, which is why the brainstem answers it by driving faster, deeper breathing.

Text: Of everything that can block a patient's airway, the most common is the {{c1::tongue::structure}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: when a patient loses consciousness the tongue relaxes and sags posteriorly, and the relaxed tongue can cover the opening of the trachea.

Pitfall: nobody actually swallows his tongue, and because the blockage is purely positional a manual airway maneuver alone reopens it.

Text: An adult is found unconscious and face-up with no trauma and nothing visible in his mouth, yet his own tongue is obstructing his airway. What relieves it? {{c1::a manual airway maneuver::technique}}
Back Extra:
Why: an unconscious patient loses the muscle tone that holds the tongue forward, so the tongue sags back over the opening of the trachea.

Pitfall: nobody actually swallows the tongue, and because the blockage is purely positional a manual technique alone relieves it.

Text: Trauma can stop a patient's breathing by injuring the {{c1::phrenic nerve::nerve}}, which drives the {{c2::diaphragm::muscle}} to contract and start inspiration, or by damaging the {{c3::brainstem::brain region}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the phrenic nerve is the wire and the brainstem is the command center, so cutting either one leaves perfectly healthy lungs unventilated.

Pitfall: neuromuscular disease such as cerebral palsy interrupts the same brain-to-diaphragm signalling with no injury at all.

Text: A soccer player is knocked unconscious by a blow to the head and has no chest or airway injury. Which half of breathing is directly threatened? {{c1::ventilation::ventilation or respiration}}
Back Extra:
Why: a depressed level of consciousness by itself impairs the movement of air, so any condition that renders a patient unconscious has a direct effect on ventilation.

Distinguish: respiration is the other half of breathing, gas crossing the alveolar membrane, and it can fail even while the patient is moving plenty of air.

Text: Gas exchange is blocked when {{c1::fluid}} fills the alveoli and when the {{c1::mucus and pus}} of pneumonia coat them, because in neither case does gas reach the alveolar surface.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: fluid in the interstitial space between the lung cells does the damage differently, widening the gap from alveolus to capillary so gas still crosses but far too slowly.

Pitfall: air can be moving in and out perfectly well while gas exchange fails, because the barrier sits at the membrane rather than in the airway.

Text: When a clot plugs a branch of the pulmonary arteries, that lung segment is still {{c1::ventilated::ventilated or perfused}} but no longer {{c1::perfused::ventilated or perfused}}, so it exchanges no gas.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: pulmonary contusion is the mirror image, where blood still flows past a bruised, fluid-filled segment that can no longer be ventilated.

Why: gas exchange needs air on one side of the membrane and blood on the other, so losing either one makes that segment contribute nothing.

Text: Respiratory function is summed up by the {{c1::ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio::measurement}}, which sets the gas actually moved through the lungs against the blood actually flowing past the alveoli.
Back Extra:
Meaning: the V is ventilation, the gas moved through the lungs, and the Q is perfusion, the blood flowing around the alveoli.

Pitfall: a mismatch means only one of the two has gone wrong, so a lung segment can be beautifully ventilated and still exchange nothing when no blood reaches it.

Text:
Sort each cause of respiratory compromise into its category:
Injury to the chest wall is a {{c1::ventilation::ventilation / respiration / oxygenation}} problem
Fluid filling the alveoli is a {{c1::respiration::ventilation / respiration / oxygenation}} problem
Toxins in the inhaled air are an {{c1::oxygenation::ventilation / respiration / oxygenation}} problem
Back Extra:
Distinguish: ventilation is moving air in and out, respiration is gas crossing the alveolar membrane, and oxygenation is the quality of the air the patient is breathing.

Pitfall: weakened respiratory muscles land under ventilation too, even though nothing is wrong with the lungs themselves.

Text: Respiratory compromise from an oxygenation problem starts in the air itself: too little {{c1::oxygen}}, too much {{c1::carbon dioxide}}, or {{c1::toxins}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: too little oxygen or too much carbon dioxide slows diffusion across the membrane, while inhaled toxins instead wreck the blood's ability to carry oxygen at all.

Ex: a fire displaces the oxygen out of the air and high altitude lowers its pressure, and both starve the alveoli before the lungs themselves are touched.

Text: A patient who cannot {{c1::exhale::inhale or exhale}} effectively builds up carbon dioxide in the blood, while a patient who cannot {{c1::inhale::inhale or exhale}} effectively has falling blood oxygen.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: exhaling is how carbon dioxide leaves the body, so trapping it raises the blood level, and inhaling is how fresh oxygen arrives, so failing to draw it in drops the blood level.

Distinguish: damage to the brain's breathing centers produces neither pattern cleanly and instead makes the rate and pattern erratic.

Text: In shock (systemic hypoperfusion), too little blood volume or a heart that pumps poorly is failure of the {{c1::central::central or peripheral}} circulation, while an inability to control blood vessel size is failure of the {{c1::peripheral::central or peripheral}} circulation.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: oxygen delivery rests on red blood cell (hemoglobin) concentration, oxygen saturation, and cardiac output, and impairing any one of the three produces shock.

Why: poor delivery starves cells of oxygen, which forces anaerobic metabolism, lactic acid production, and finally organ dysfunction.
